youth noun

young people; a young man

also the youth, young people, a youth, youths, youngsters, teenager, teenagers, young lady, youngster

classical

Cic. Sen. 28: studiīs juventūtis
Traupman 410

juventūs, juventūtis f.

noun, third declension · Declension on Wiktionary

young people, the youth (collectively)

The usual sense of the word: the young men of a city or a people taken together (Lewis & Short). For the time of life, see youth (the time of being young).

Other words

  • adulēscēns, adulēscentis m./f. — a youth, a young man or woman

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Cic. Sen. 38: adulēscentem in quō est senīle aliquid; Traupman 78: young lady, adulēscēns f. · Declension on Wiktionary

    One young person, of the age of adulēscentia, about fifteen to thirty (Lewis & Short); see young. In the plural, young people.

  • adulēscentulus, adulēscentulī m. — a very young man, a lad

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Traupman 78, 410 · Declension on Wiktionary

    The diminutive: in Terence and Cicero; Cicero calls himself adulēscentulus at twenty-seven (Or. 30). It can sound slighting, “a mere lad” (Lewis & Short).

  • muliercula, mulierculae f. — a little woman, a mere woman

    noun, first declension · avoid · classical · Lucr. 4.1279 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 78: young lady, muliercula; Traupman 410 · Declension on Wiktionary

    Traupman gives it for “young lady”, but the diminutive of mulier belittles (Lewis & Short: “a little woman, mere woman”). Say adulēscēns or puella.

Examples

  • quid enim est jūcundius senectūte stīpātā studiīs juventūtis?

    for what is more delightful than an old age surrounded by eager young people?Cic. Sen. 28

  • ut enim adulēscentem in quō est senīle aliquid, sīc senem in quō est aliquid adulēscentis probō

    for as I like a young man who has something of the old in him, so I like an old man who has something of the youngCic. Sen. 38

See also youth, young, generation, child, old.
